strategy: Prioritize the stateful, single-replica Redis cart dependency because it spans every flow and prior Redis unavailability caused a frontend-silence guard abort; use a short pod kill to measure recovery behavior. Then test partial packet loss on the checkout-only payment path and CPU contention on the recommendation service, covering three distinct failure classes without repeating established experiments.

spec.reason: Ranked first because redis-cart is a single-replica stateful dependency holding cart data, with reach 1.0 across all five flows. A prior pod_failure on redis-cart caused frontend unresponsiveness and a guard abort; a pod kill tests the distinct recovery path and whether the cart state and dependent flows recover.
spec.hypothesis: With Redis unavailable during replacement, cart operations and dependent requests will be disrupted across the shop; Kubernetes will eventually restore the pod, but the user-flow guard is likely to abort before the full 30 seconds.

experiments.learning_goal: How quickly does the stateful cart dependency recover after pod replacement, and what is the user-visible blast radius while it is recovering?

spec.reason: paymentservice is a single-replica dependency on the revenue path, with checkout as its only mapped user flow. Prior pod_failure runs showed checkout errors near the guard threshold, but partial network loss on this service has not been tested; 5% loss probes retry and timeout behavior at a restrained intensity.
spec.hypothesis: A small share of dropped packets will primarily affect checkout through retries or occasional failed payment calls, while other flows remain unaffected; the low loss rate should stay below the guard thresholds.

experiments.learning_goal: Does intermittent packet loss on the payment dependency cause checkout errors, retry-driven latency, or both?

spec.reason: recommendationservice is a single-replica service reached by product, view_cart, and checkout flows, and has a 200m CPU limit. Its prior network-delay run affected those flows, but CPU contention has not been tested on it; this gives a distinct resource-pressure/slowdown measurement outside the already well-characterized frontend load tests.
spec.hypothesis: CPU contention will increase latency on requests waiting for recommendations in product, view_cart, and checkout, without causing broad errors; the short, sub-maximal stress should remain below the safety guard.

experiments.learning_goal: How sensitive are recommendation-dependent flows to CPU contention, and does the service remain available under a brief CPU load?

skipped_ideas.idea: Repeat 100 ms network delay on productcatalogservice
skipped_ideas.why_not: Multiple past runs consistently showed severe slowdown across all flows; repeating the same intensity would add little new information.

skipped_ideas.idea: Traffic spike at 300 users on frontend
skipped_ideas.why_not: Repeated runs already crossed the 1500 ms p95 guard at this load. A further test is unlikely to teach more than the existing capacity-threshold evidence.

skipped_ideas.idea: Memory stress on cartservice near its 128 Mi limit
skipped_ideas.why_not: A 110 MB memory-stress run already caused broad high errors, an abort, and a restart; repeating this destructive resource-exhaustion experiment is lower value than testing new failure classes.
